question: I need to know a good quick summary of the Microsoft document or the research whatever it said about how the more context and continuity you give to an agent the better it's gonna help the human, I'm trying to make this case in a meeting next week and I need to be able to pull easily from the relevant statistics or research and whatever Microsoft has got that's like visually interesting and helpful for this
answer:
Short direct answer (for your meeting): Yes — Microsoft’s report and the studies it cites show that giving agents more conversational context and continuity (multi‑turn history, persistent state, multi‑turn-aware rewards) measurably improves how useful they are to people — but only when the extra context is exposed and managed with good UX and alignment. Evidence in the report: an LLM facilitator raised information sharing (~+22% vs none), multi‑turn-aware rewards boosted task success (~+18.5%) and user satisfaction (~+17.6%), and prototype systems report clear gains on multi‑turn collaboration metrics. (Sources and figures below.)

If you meant something specific by “more context / continuity”:
- If you mean “more multi‑turn history during one session” — the report directly supports this: multi‑turn context + multi‑turn rewards improves collaboration and outcomes (see Wu et al. 2025 / COLLABLLM, page 44).
- If you mean “continuity across sessions / persistent memory” — the report argues the same principles apply (reasoning about past actions and predicting behaviour improves collaboration) but most cited experiments focus on multi‑turn dialogue/session continuity; persistent-memory results are discussed conceptually rather than with the same numeric benchmarks.
- If you mean “more raw info without UX changes” — caution: the report warns that more context can overwhelm humans unless interfaces surface the right highlights (page 29).

Key evidence and ready-to‑use lines (with source, page):
- “AI facilitators boosted a measure of information sharing by 22% over no facilitation” — Alsobay et al. (2025) experiment reported in New-Future-Of-Work-Report-2025.pdf, page 41. Use as a short punchline: “+22% information sharing with an LLM facilitator vs no facilitator (Alsobay et al., 2025; Microsoft report p.41).”
- “A multi‑turn reward function boosted task success by 18.5% and user satisfaction by 17.6%” — Wu et al. (2025) / COLLABLLM reported in the Microsoft report (page 44). Slide text: “Multi‑turn-aware rewards → +18.5% task success, +17.6% user satisfaction (Wu et al., 2025; MS report p.44).”
- Prototype metrics illustrating multi‑turn benefits: COLLABLLM example shows “High Quality (BLEU=0.46); High Efficiency (1.39k tokens read); High Interactivity (LLM Judge score=0.8)” (page 44) — good for a visual/metric to show “measurable prototype gains.”

Relevant visuals from the report (use in slides):
- Visual that directly shows the experimental result (LLM facilitator producing more facts over time). This is a clear, presentation-ready chart to show the effect size over time:
  ![Source figure](fli-image:report-document:1:233)
  Why it helps: empirical, multi‑condition line chart showing the LLM facilitator (red) pulling ahead of human/no facilitation — good to illustrate the +22% information‑sharing claim.
  What it does not establish: it’s from a specific lab task; it shows increased information sharing but not necessarily improved final decisions (the paper reports sharing ↑ but decision outcomes were not changed).
  Source: New-Future-Of-Work-Report-2025.pdf, page 41 (summary of Alsobay et al., 2025).
- Conceptual flow / metric panel for multi‑turn / continuity improvements (illustrates how history → collaborative simulation → better future turns and includes prototype metrics):
  ![Source figure](fli-image:report-document:1:236)
  Why it helps: shows the mechanism Microsoft highlights — keeping history and simulating future turns (collaborative simulation + RL finetuning) transforms models into more proactive “team members.” The small metric panel (BLEU, tokens read, LLM judge) gives quick numbers for slides.
  What it does not establish: conceptual/experimental prototype results — not a field trial of long‑term persistent memory across real users.
- (Optional for oversight/UX point) Tree-style reasoning visualization — use if you want to argue that more context needs better interfaces:
  ![Source figure](fli-image:report-document:1:228)
  Why it helps: shows how visualizing chain-of-thought and branching decisions makes multi‑turn reasoning inspectable and actionable for humans (supports the “context only helps if you make it observable” claim).
  What it does not establish: purely a UX illustration; not a numeric result.

Short script you can read in the meeting (30–45 seconds):
- “Recent Microsoft research and experiments show a consistent theme: when agents hold more conversational context and are trained/optimized for multi‑turn collaboration, people get more help. For example, an LLM facilitator condition produced about 22% more information sharing than no facilitator (Alsobay et al., 2025; MS report p.41), and a multi‑turn reward design increased task success by ~18.5% and user satisfaction by ~17.6% (Wu et al., 2025; MS report p.44). But Microsoft cautions that extra context must be surfaced with good UX and transparency, otherwise it overloads oversight (New-Future-Of-Work-Report-2025, p.29).”

Important qualifiers and caveats (so you don’t overclaim):
- These numbers come from specific controlled experiments and prototype systems summarized in Microsoft’s New Future of Work Report (2025) and the underlying working papers (Alsobay et al., Wu et al., etc.). They are promising but context‑dependent — task design, participant pool and how “facilitation” is implemented matter.
- The report repeatedly flags human oversight and explainability as essential: more context is useful only if interfaces help people find the relevant information (p.29).
- Many cited items are working papers / arXiv / prototypes (2024–2025). Treat them as strong evidence of direction, not final field‑tested standards.

If you’d like, I can:
- Produce a single slide (title, two bullets, one chart image [figure p.41], one small caption with source + one‑line caveat) sized for your deck.
- Provide the exact one‑sentence citation line to put on your slide: e.g., “Alsobay et al., 2025 (summarized in Microsoft, New Future of Work Report 2025, p.41).”
Tell me whether you want the single-slide image formatted for PowerPoint (I can draft the slide text and image choices and keep it concise).

Effective oversight of agents likely requires UX innovations for transparency

· Human oversight of agentic Al systems requires knowledge and observability. It requires knowledge about the capabilities, limitations, and workings of the system, as well as domain expertise and situational awareness to enable intervention. And it requires observability of system activity, decisions, and outputs (Bansal et al., 2024; Passi, 2025; Shavit et al., 2023).

· Whether human oversight happens as real-time monitoring or post-hoc auditing, it is very challenging. Information volume, complexity, and speed make it tremendously difficult for people to exercise meaningful human oversight (Holzinger et al., 2024; Lane et al., 2024; Passi, 2025).

· Three sociotechnical challenges compound the difficulty of human oversight:

· Agentic systems struggle with the goal-plan-execution gap, arising from mismatches between how users describe goals to systems, how systems interpret and plan for user goals, and how these plans fare in real-world contexts.

· Through facilitation agents appearing in online meeting platforms, people are increasingly exposed to AI meeting participants that track time, summarize meetings, and more (e.g., Microsoft's Facilitator Agent, and Zoom's Al Companion).

· Alsobay et al. (2025) compared Al and human facilitation in a group task in which participants have different information that must be shared to reach a decision. Al facilitators boosted a measure of information sharing by 22% over no facilitation and were perceived favorably by participants. However, neither human nor Al facilitators changed group decisions, suggesting that outcome- shaping may require tools that additionally target decision-making processes (e.g. Chiang et al., 2024).

· Al agents can also support more inclusive meetings by observing interactions, asking for users' perspectives, and intervening when appropriate. However, as with decision-making, outcome-shaping is hard, because while people prefer agents to ask before intervening, they may also rationalize away their input (Houtti et al., 2025).

· Standard RLHF-inspired alignment techniques that are essential to the success of Al models (e.g., PPO, DPO) fail to maintain reliability in extended multi-turn (Laban et al., 2025) and multi-party dialogues (Nath et al., 2025a; 2025b) because they assume static, single-user interactions and optimize for narrow, turn-level rewards (Wu et al., 2025).

· Wu et al. (2025) highlight the limitations of traditional alignment methods that optimize for single-turn correctness and immediate user satisfaction, and propose a multi-turn reward function that evaluates responses based on their long-term impact on collaboration, boosting task success by 18.5% and user satisfaction by 17.6%.

· Nath et al. (2025a) show that standard alignment techniques lose their reliability in long multi-turn, multi-party conversations, as these methods assume a static mapping from the agent's action to the outcome and fail to account for the complexity of group conversations where each participant can alter the course of those actions.

COLLABLLM incorporates multiturn-aware rewards from collaborative simulation, enabling forward-looking strategies (Wu et al., 2025).

· Nath et al. (2025b) propose a "Frictional Agent Alignment Framework" that explicitly models conversation state and frictive conditions (Clark, 1996), accounts for group dynamics where collaborator responses can alter effects of intervention, and optimizes for collaborative processes like common-ground construction and deliberation.

This report is a product of Microsoft's New Future of Work Initiative

Microsoft has shaped information work for over 50 years and the New Future of Work (NFW) initiative has helped it navigate the past five years of profound transformation. While the initiative was born out of the COVID-19 pandemic and subsequent shifts to remote and hybrid work, since 2023 it has focused on the incorporation and growing role of tools powered by large AI models.

Throughout this transformative period, the NFW initiative has brought together researchers from across Microsoft to conduct primary research and synthesize existing findings from the literature. The goal is not merely to predict what changes are coming, but to actively create a new future of work that is equitable, inclusive, meaningful, and productive.

The fifth edition of the annual NFW report represents another year of research and analysis, adding to the growing body of knowledge on Al and work. The evidence and insights presented here are not monolithic and represent contributing researchers' perspectives rather than Microsoft's corporate views. Additional research papers, practical guides, and white papers are available at: aka.ms/nfw.

Overview

Workstreams Publications Videos News & features

The New Future of Work is a cross-company research initiative dedicated to creating solutions for a future of work that is meaningful, productive, and equitable. It began during the pandemic in response to an urgent need to understand remote work practices. When many people returned to the office, the focus shifted to supporting the hybrid work transition. Then in 2023, another generational shift in work occurred when language models made the leap from the lab into the real world, a shift that could make the changes to remote and hybrid work look small by comparison.

The future of work with Al is not a forgone conclusion, and this initiative exists to not just study work with Al, but to help Microsoft build a new future of work with Al that empowers every person on the planet.

This site features research from the initiative that has been published in peer-reviewed scientific venues, as well as resources to help you navigate a rapidly changing work environment and thrive in the age of Al. We recently published our 2024 Report that summarizes some of the exciting work in this space.

AI facilitation can boost information-sharing and inclusion, though shaping decision outcomes remains challenging

· Through facilitation agents appearing in online meeting platforms, people are increasingly exposed to AI meeting participants that track time, summarize meetings, and more (e.g., Microsoft's Facilitator Agent, and Zoom's Al Companion).

· Alsobay et al. (2025) compared Al and human facilitation in a group task in which participants have different information that must be shared to reach a decision. Al facilitators boosted a measure of information sharing by 22% over no facilitation and were perceived favorably by participants. However, neither human nor Al facilitators changed group decisions, suggesting that outcome- shaping may require tools that additionally target decision-making processes (e.g. Chiang et al., 2024).

· Al agents can also support more inclusive meetings by observing interactions, asking for users' perspectives, and intervening when appropriate. However, as with decision-making, outcome-shaping is hard, because while people prefer agents to ask before intervening, they may also rationalize away their input (Houtti et al., 2025).

Effective oversight of agents likely requires UX innovations for transparency

· Human oversight of agentic Al systems requires knowledge and observability. It requires knowledge about the capabilities, limitations, and workings of the system, as well as domain expertise and situational awareness to enable intervention. And it requires observability of system activity, decisions, and outputs (Bansal et al., 2024; Passi, 2025; Shavit et al., 2023).

· Whether human oversight happens as real-time monitoring or post-hoc auditing, it is very challenging. Information volume, complexity, and speed make it tremendously difficult for people to exercise meaningful human oversight (Holzinger et al., 2024; Lane et al., 2024; Passi, 2025).

· Three sociotechnical challenges compound the difficulty of human oversight:

· Agentic systems struggle with the goal-plan-execution gap, arising from mismatches between how users describe goals to systems, how systems interpret and plan for user goals, and how these plans fare in real-world contexts.

A tree visualization of the reasoning steps in a chain-of-thought process designed to help people understand and provided feedback to an AI system (Pang et al. 2025).

· Spotting mistakes from agentic systems is a formidable task that can be akin to finding the needle in the haystack.

· What is useful to observe in the workings of agentic systems is contextual.

· UX improvements are needed to reduce the burden of human oversight, such as: curating and organizing information, enabling interactive sensemaking, using visual summaries, and highlighting real-time changes. Dynamic, personalized interfaces are a promising direction (Wang & Lu, 2025).

This report is a product of Microsoft's New Future of Work Initiative

Microsoft has shaped information work for over 50 years and the New Future of Work (NFW) initiative has helped it navigate the past five years of profound transformation. While the initiative was born out of the COVID-19 pandemic and subsequent shifts to remote and hybrid work, since 2023 it has focused on the incorporation and growing role of tools powered by large AI models.

Throughout this transformative period, the NFW initiative has brought together researchers from across Microsoft to conduct primary research and synthesize existing findings from the literature. The goal is not merely to predict what changes are coming, but to actively create a new future of work that is equitable, inclusive, meaningful, and productive.

The fifth edition of the annual NFW report represents another year of research and analysis, adding to the growing body of knowledge on Al and work. The evidence and insights presented here are not monolithic and represent contributing researchers' perspectives rather than Microsoft's corporate views. Additional research papers, practical guides, and white papers are available at: aka.ms/nfw.
